newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Grain-Trade sees record wheat crop.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Grain-Trade sees record wheat crop.

text.p: Australia's 1996/97 wheat harvest looks like coming in at up to 24 million tonnes, far ahead of most estimates, Guy Allen, grain trading manager for GrainCorp, the leading grain handling cooperative in New South Wales, said.
Other traders agreed that the Australian crop could exceed the previous record of 22 million tonnes, set in 1983/84.
With the harvest 95 percent complete, GrainCorp had received more than eight million tonnes into its system in New South Wales (NSW), Allen told Reuters.
"This is significantly larger than expected. It (the national harvest) could approach 24 million tonnes for wheat.
"I think it's definitely over 23 (million tonnes)," he said.
Wheat quality was very good, with little feed wheat and off-grade grain in a quickly-delivered harvest, he said.
"It's just been an exceptional year," he said.

Bill Mitchell of New England Agricultural Traders, a division of Geneva-based international wheat trader Romak, said the way the harvest had been going raised a good chance that a 22 million tonne wheat harvest would be met or exceeded.

Latest official forecasts for Australia's bumper wheat crop have settled at about the 21.5 million tonne mark, after months of successive increases. The Australian Wheat Board forecasts 21.5 million tonnes, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics 21.3 million tonnes and private forecaster Australian Wheat Forecasters Pty Ltd 21.37 million tonnes.

AWF principal Brian Bailey said he did not agree with the view that Australia was headed for a record crop. High receivals into the grain handling system indicated that less grain than usual was being held on farm because quality of the present crop was most suited to the export trade, he said.
However, the view that Australia could have a record wheat crop was circulating in sections of the trade, he said.
While wheat rolls into Australia's domestic system, NSW exports slowed last week because of shipping problems.
Delays occurred in some ship arrivals, while high seas at Newcastle port in NSW stopped ships reaching port, Allen said.
Port Adelaide, however, on Friday was loading 42,000 tonnes of wheat onto an Iran-bound vessel, a new record for the port.
The main feature on Australian domestic markets last week was a heavy delivery schedule into Sydney futures, with deliveries taking place on about 600 contracts.
While the system coped well with the deliveries on about 600 contracts, futures trading virtually stopped.
No trades took place on four of the five market days, while the 58 trades which did occur on Wednesday mostly involved rollovers from the January into the March contract.
Allen saw cash markets as a little firmer over the past week, with Newcastle delivered Australian Standard White (ASW) rising by about A$5.00 a tonne to A$160.00-A$162.00 a tonne.
End user demand for January shipment could limit late deliveries into the futures market in the coming week, he said.
Cash sorghum last week was steady to a little firmer, with bids at A$140.00 a tonne Newcastle and A$145.00 a tonne Sydney in limited activity, with producers on post-harvest holiday.
Mitchell saw cash markets as steady and dull in the past week amid the holiday season and an international news vacuum.
